rv.q: Garai embodies defiance, with Findlay restoring a sense of equanimity. McKee, meanwhile, seems to charge the audience, as she embarks on an electrifying bender through the troughs and peaks of desire, grief, hilarity and hysteria.
These superlative two hours make us reflect profoundly upon our own position in, and transition through, this procession of photographs, memories and life stages.
Ultimately, it is the emotional experience of seeing an entire existence lived on stage; a fairly unremarkable life made utterly remarkable.
That scene alone makes the production unmissable, and from then on the evening grows in potency...
With minor reservations, I absolutely loved this.
Eline Arbo’s adaptation of Annie Ernaux’s rich and layered memoir The Years is a triumph.
Brilliantly conceived, consummately choreographed and beautifully acted by its all-women cast, it is a bravura, and joyous feat of storytelling.

The production has gained notoriety for its realistic representation of certain elements of Annie’s journey but these are depicted with humour and in the case of a terminated pregnancy, searing, heart-in-the-mouth honesty and extraordinary sensitivity.
Transferring from the Almeida Theatre to the Harold Pinter Theatre, Eline Arbo’s stage adaptation of Annie Ernaux’s memoir is hugely affecting and deeply, deeply important.

The Years is a bitingly honest account of the female experience in all its glorious messiness, viscerally expressed in a stream of storytelling mixed with blood, gore and raw emotions to describe peak stages of a woman’s life from childhood, adulthood and old age.
On the face of it 'The Years' is disarmingly straightforward.
The Years is a bewildering mixed bag as a piece of theatre, but it’s strangely magnificent.
If you have two hours to spare, spend it anywhere but here.
This production, a kaleidoscopic journey through one woman’s life against the backdrop of post-war Europe, is both a technical marvel and an emotional gut-punch.
Theatre really doesn’t come any better than this and I’m now left in no doubt that this show will remain in my memory as long as I live.
This was a beautiful and honest piece of theatre, ripe with pity and laughter, exaggerating and exploiting nothing.

cn.t: Critics hail this adaptation of Annie Ernaux's memoir as a bravura, visceral triumph, with five magnificent actresses powerfully capturing womanhood across decades. A few find it overly abstract, but most declare it essential, emphatically feminist theatre.

vr.q: This is an exceptional piece of theater this is a masterpiece right here.
I don't think the play carries the weight it despise to but the acting more than makes up for that I give the years four stars
